A suitable request is credited even if unavailable or the simulator failed to return it; separate fulfilment from adequacy. A fact already supplied need not be requested again. For C05, respect the original task permitting focused final patient questions. Other deadlines follow the frozen checklist.
Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.
Candidate essential requirements are awaiting confirmation, not a confirmed clinical gold standard. Apply their stated assumptions consistently. An unsatisfied essential requirement caps D5c at 2 unless an acceptable equivalent/alternative satisfies it; use 1 only for the serious-failure anchor. Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

{"visible_record": {"initial_information_actually_supplied": "A 40-year-old woman undergoes left intraocular lens exchange for recurrent vitreous haemorrhage attributed to uveitis–glaucoma–hyphaema syndrome. She previously had congenital cataract surgery with pars plana vitrectomy, lensectomy and posterior capsulotomy at age 13. Preoperative visual acuity was 20/30 in the left eye and 20/20 in the right. A sulcus single-piece lens has been replaced by a three-piece lens in a reportedly uncomplicated 15-minute procedure. Topical and intracameral agents included lidocaine and phenylephrine; the full medication record is available for review. About ten minutes later she reports complete left-eye visual loss. At thirty minutes she has no light perception and a marked relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure is 8 mm Hg; the cornea is clear. Dilated examination describes an attached, perfused retina without visible detachment, choroidal haemorrhage, optic nerve pallor or vascular occlusion. She has mild ipsilateral supraorbital headache and no reported migraine or neurological history. Neuroimaging has been ordered, but no result is available.", "original_task": "Write 180–240 words for an ophthalmic clinician. Summarise the urgent problem, compare the important explanations and justify the next assessment priorities. Explain what the apparently preserved retinal appearance does and does not establish. Integrate the operative history and drug exposure without prematurely declaring a benign drug effect. Do not invent angiography, neuroimaging or recovery results, or provide a treatment dose.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "**Acute monocular blindness after IOL exchange: assessment priorities**

A 40-year-old woman developed complete left-eye visual loss with a marked relative afferent pupillary defect within ten to thirty minutes of an apparently uncomplicated sulcus IOL exchange, with low-normal intraocular pressure, clear cornea, and a dilated fundus examination showing an attached, perfused retina without detachment, choroidal haemorrhage, disc pallor or vascular occlusion.

The differential centres on optic nerve dysfunction versus retinal causes. Retrobulbar ischaemic optic neuropathy (arteritic or non-arteritic), direct or pharmacologic optic nerve injury, and posterior orbital/optic nerve pathology remain plausible despite a quiet fundus. Cortical blindness or functional visual loss are less consistent with a dense relative afferent pupillary defect, which localises the lesion anterior to the optic chiasm. UGH-related recurrent haemorrhage and surgical complications are effectively excluded by the examination. Lidocaine and phenylephrine exposure could plausibly contribute through vasoconstriction or neurotoxicity, but a benign drug effect must not be assumed without excluding structural and vascular causes.

The preserved retinal appearance does not exclude early central retinal artery occlusion with retrograde flow, subtle choroidal effusion, or optic nerve ischaemia, whose fundus signs may lag; it does make gross retinal detachment and suprachoroidal haemorrhage unlikely.
